Chapter 7: The Power of Collective Action.
You know, real change almost never arrives in a thunderclap. Most of the time, it starts with just a handful of folks who can’t sit quietly with the way things are. Maybe they gather in someone’s living room, or the corner of a church basement, or even an online forum late at night. They swap stories, imagine what could be different, and take those first small steps—an after-school program, a petition, maybe a protest.
At first, it all seems so tiny, right? But bit by bit, those little acts build up. Before long, momentum catches, and more people start to notice—and join in.
Picture this: a group of tenants, tired of sky-high rents and rundown buildings, decide they’ve had enough. So, they start with something simple—knocking on their neighbors’ doors, just listening. In the beginning, lots of folks are doubtful. Someone might say, “Nothing ever changes.” But as the group grows, you can feel the shift. Confidence starts to take root. They pick up skills—how to negotiate, talk to the press, push back against landlords who don’t deliver. Wins might come slowly, but every victory, no matter how small, makes the next one just a bit easier.
See, collective action isn’t just about gathering a crowd. It’s about building relationships, learning to trust, and figuring out how to work together—even when it’s messy. Let’s be honest, most of us didn’t learn these things in school. We pick them up by jumping in, making mistakes, listening more than we talk, and showing up even when it’s tough.
The process? It’s unpredictable, sometimes frustrating, but always rewarding.
Of course, it’s not all smooth sailing. Campaigns might fail. Leaders get burned out. Sometimes, coalitions just fall apart. And in those moments, hope can feel pretty far away. But if you look back at history, you’ll see it’s full of people who kept going. When one effort stumbles, another rises. Lessons learned from losses? They often plant the seeds for future wins.
Over time, it becomes clear: collective action isn’t just about passing new policies or winning elections. It’s about shifting how people relate to one another. When folks come together, they start to see themselves differently—not just as individuals, but as part of something bigger. That sense of isolation and powerlessness? It gets replaced by a new sense of agency and belonging.
Here’s something to keep in mind: most of us underestimate our own power. It’s so easy to believe that change is something that happens “out there,” led by experts or leaders we’ll never meet. But the truth? Every movement for justice has been built by regular people, taking small steps together.
The real power of collective action is in turning private pain into a shared purpose—transforming despair into hope.
And the story isn’t over. Every single day, new groups form, fresh alliances spring up, and new possibilities take shape. The work is challenging, sure, but it’s always worth it.
In a world that often feels divided and exclusive, collective action is the path toward something better.
